title: Power
summary: Main breaker trips, brownouts, Kraken current limits, loose PDH and breaker terminals, battery.

options.label: Main breaker tripped in a match
Robot is dead, no lights anywhere
One device or channel has no power
Radio or RIO reboots when the robot drives
PDH status light is not green

drive-motors.question: Does the drivetrain use Kraken X60 or Falcon (Talon FX) motors?

kraken-limits.title: Main breaker trip: Kraken supply current limits
steps: Nearly every main breaker trip this season was Kraken or Falcon drive motors left on the default 70 A supply current limit. Eight swerve motors at 70 A is far more than the 120 A main breaker holds.
Ask the team to set SupplyCurrentLimit on the drive motors to 50 to 60 A with SupplyCurrentLimitEnable true. Steer motors 20 to 30 A. Check the limits in Phoenix Tuner X config after deploy.
A stator limit (default 120 A) does not protect the breaker on its own. The supply limit is the one that matters here.
Check the breaker lugs. Try to rotate each crimped lug. If it turns, tighten the nut. A hot loose lug trips early.
Redeploy, run the drivetrain against a wall for a few seconds, and watch total current in the DS log or PDH.
Still tripping after lower limits: check the breaker age and the battery leads, then call the CSA.

main-breaker-other.title: Main breaker trip: other causes
steps: Try to rotate each lug on the main breaker by hand. If it turns, the nut is loose. Tighten it. Loose lugs heat the breaker and it trips below rating.
Check the battery connector and the battery leads. Wiggle them. Tie-wrap the connector halves together.
Ask what the robot was doing when it tripped. Stalled arm, pinned drivetrain, or a mechanism against a hard stop draws full stall current.
Set supply current limits on every drive and mechanism motor. Spark MAX: smart current limit 40 to 60 A on drive. Talon FX: supply limit 50 to 60 A.
Breakers age. One that has tripped many times trips easier. Swap it for a new 120 A breaker.
Call the CSA if the team cannot find where the current goes.

battery-voltage.question: What does the DS show for battery voltage with the robot disabled and resting?

weak-battery.title: Weak battery
steps: Swap to a fully charged battery. A good battery rests at 12.5 V or more.
Ask if the battery has been dropped or is more than 2 seasons old. Retire it.
Check the battery leads and connector. A loose crimp reads low under load even on a full battery.
Use a battery beak or load tester if the team has one. Under 12.0 V loaded means retire it.
Tell the team to charge every battery before each match.

brownout-wiring.title: Brownout with a good battery
steps: Open the DS log. Find the voltage dip. Under 6.8 V the RIO starts cutting outputs. Under 6.3 V (RIO 1) or 6.75 V (RIO 2 default) everything disables.
Wiggle the battery connector and main breaker lugs. Try to rotate each lug. Loose main power is the most common cause after motors.
Squeeze the wires at the PDH or PDP main terminals. Confirm the bolts are tight with split washers.
Lower motor supply current limits. Drive first, then any mechanism that starts from stall.
Check the RIO is on its own channel. A shared channel with a motor pulls it down.
Escalate to the CSA if the dip happens with all motors idle.

dead.question: Is the main breaker pushed in and the battery connector fully mated?

dead-fixed.title: Breaker or battery was not connected
steps: Push the main breaker in until it clicks. Mate the battery connector until it seats.
Tie-wrap the battery connector halves together so it cannot pull apart in a match.
Check the breaker lever does not sit half way. A tripped breaker sits between on and off.

dead-robot.title: Robot dead with breaker in and battery connected
steps: Check the battery with a meter at the terminals. Under 10 V is a dead battery. Swap it.
Measure from the battery through the breaker to the PDH or PDP. No voltage after the breaker means a dead breaker or a broken lug crimp.
Look at the PDH or PDP status LED. Dark with 12 V on the main terminals means the board is dead or reverse polarity.
Check for a wire that pulled out of the main terminal or a broken battery lead crimp.
Swap the breaker. If the PDH stays dark, call the CSA.

channel.title: One channel has no power
steps: On the PDH, a red channel LED means no voltage and a fault. Check the breaker is pushed in all the way or the fuse is seated.
A blinking red channel LED is a sticky fault from an earlier trip. Push the breaker in and clear faults.
Tug the Weidmuller wires on that channel. Pull, strip, and reseat.
Swap the breaker or fuse with a known good one of the same rating.
On the PDH, the switchable channel is off until code turns it on. Check the team is not using it for something that must always be on.

reboot-under-load.title: Radio or RIO reboots under load
steps: Squeeze and wiggle the wires at the PDH or PDP main terminals and the main breaker. A loose terminal drops voltage when motors pull current.
Tug the RIO and radio power plugs. Reseat with fresh stripped copper. Tie-wrap the cables.
If the radio has PoE and DC power at the same time, remove one.
Check the DS log for the voltage dip. Under 6.3 V the RIO can reset. Lower motor supply current limits.
Put the RIO and radio on their own channels. Not shared with a motor or compressor.
Still rebooting: swap the battery, then the breaker. Call the CSA.

pdh-lights.title: PDH status light
steps: Blue solid: powered, no CAN comms. Check the CAN wires and that robot code is running.
Orange and yellow blinking: CAN fault. Check the bus and the PDH termination jumper.
Orange and blue blinking: low battery. Swap the battery.
Orange and magenta blinking: over current on the board. Find the stalled device.
Magenta blinking: keep alive timeout. Code stopped talking to it. Restart robot code.
Use the Status Lights reference for the full table. Call the CSA for a hardware fault (orange and cyan).
